title: Simulating Supply and Demand
beats: One buyer, one seller, grow to many; then argue for and against markets
Blue blobs sell rockets, orange blobs buy; value shown as a bar
Seller bar is minimum price, buyer bar is maximum; any price between works
Buyer max $40, seller min $20, trade at $30; each gains $10, named surplus
Pause: value is slippery, but comparing alternatives quantifies it
Add a second buyer with lower limit; list daily rules for random-order haggling and expectation adjusting
One pair: nothing changes; add buyer: what happens?
Price creeps upward; buyer competition shifts surplus to seller
Mirror case with three sellers, two buyers: price falls, buyers gain
Three and three: predict outcome; only two rockets sell
Lowest buyer and highest seller can never match, so trade count is limited
Equilibrium as quantity supplied equals demanded; supply and demand curves as shorthand for many blobs
Milestone: market built; now argue what model means
Equilibrium maximizes surplus; the next pair would give negative surplus
Efficiency and invisible hand defined as the automatic result
Regulation arguments: real markets need many participants, free exit, information
Surplus measures one blob at a time; society may weigh all blobs, citing food, labor, healthcare
Markets are tools; plug that viewing and support signal demand for videos

metrics.misconception: partial: markets are neither fundamentally good nor bad (11:40)
metrics.brute_force: yes 3:48: simulate haggling blobs rather than draw curves
metrics.examples: 1 buyer/1 seller, 2 buyers/1 seller, 2 buyers/3 sellers, 3 and 3; each adds one actor and a predict prompt
metrics.ending: Markets as a tool; humorous demand-signal plug

principles.1: confirmed: rockets, blobs, haggling before any curve (0:15)
principles.2: confirmed: surplus defined at 1:39 only after a $40/$20/$30 example; curves held until 7:39
principles.3: partly: supply/demand curves arrive as compression of many blobs (7:39), not practiced
principles.4: partly: blobs are concrete agents, but no analogy-then-rigor swap
principles.5: confirmed: blobs literally buy and sell, adjust prices daily (2:44-3:48)
principles.6: confirmed: simulate the market before curves; daily rules and tracking panel (3:48)
principles.7: confirmed: competition shifts surplus (4:08, 5:40), equilibrium emerges from repeated days
principles.8: partly: no timing evidence; idea rate slows by adding one actor at a time
principles.9: confirmed: buyer competition then seller competition mirror each other (4:08, 5:40)
principles.11: confirmed: surplus before equilibrium before curves before efficiency
principles.12: partly: only links to policy debates and food, labor, healthcare (11:07); no outside sources
principles.13: partly: simple and lists conditions for ideal markets; tool-choice justification limited

new_moves.name: mirror-experiment
new_moves.what: Run the symmetric case to show same mechanism flips the beneficiary

new_moves.name: model-then-argue
new_moves.what: After building the model, state it as a map of arguments rather than conclusions

new_moves.name: scope-the-claim
new_moves.what: Define what surplus measures and what it ignores

theory: The video adds exactly one actor per scene and asks what will happen, so the learner re-derives who benefits before a vocabulary word appears. Terms (surplus, equilibrium, curves) are bolted on after the sim has made them needed, and the final third deliberately marks the model's limits.
velocity: Scene builder: one-actor-at-a-time market scene with a live surplus tally
Voice: name a term only after the scene has displayed its value
Orchestrator: ask a prediction before each added actor
Evals: check that the tutor states what the model leaves out
quote: we just figured a way to quantify it by comparing alternatives
